posts.caption: The vet stood back on Thursday, looked at Pudding from the side, and said the words easy keeper in a tone I didn't love. So we're cutting back. Less grain, a slow feeder net, and no more handfuls of anything from my coat pocket. He took it well for about a day. Then I noticed the old apple tree in the back corner of the pasture had stopped dropping apples on the ground. Or rather, they were dropping. They just weren't staying there long. I found him under it at 7:10 this morning, waiting. He looked up like the next one was running late.
posts.first: My first pony figured out which neighbor had the crabapple tree within a week of coming home. Every escape that whole summer ended under that tree. The neighbor eventually started leaving a bucket of windfalls by the fence for him, which I'm fairly sure counts as aiding and abetting.

posts.caption: The equine dentist comes twice a year, and twice a year Big Red treats it like a hostile takeover. Last spring she let him get the speculum about halfway in before she remembered she had opinions. This time he called ahead. He parked by the wash rack instead of the barn door, walked up slowly, and kept his hands in his pockets like he was visiting a museum. She watched him the whole way. He got the job done in forty minutes, which is a record. I'm told the carrot in his coat pocket did most of the work.
posts.first: Our old dentist used to talk to every horse the entire time, low and steady, like a radio left on in the barn. I asked him once what he was saying. He said mostly the weather and what he had for lunch. It worked on every horse I ever owned.

posts.caption: The neighbor kids got a trampoline this summer and set it up about forty feet from our fence line. The younger horses lost their minds for a week. Snorting, tails up, laps of the pasture every time somebody bounced. The old gray gelding never moved. He stood under the maple with one hind leg cocked and a strand of hay hanging out of his mouth. At first I thought it was wisdom. Then on Saturday I watched him turn his head, look straight at the trampoline, and blink at it like he was seeing it for the first time.
posts.first: When I was young I rode an old school horse named Buck who had carried every kid in the county. A balloon popped right beside him at the fair once. He sighed. That was it. I've owned a lot of horses since, and I still compare every one of them to Buck.

posts.caption: I bought her as a coming three-year-old at a sale barn in 2006 with money I'd been saving for a different car. I drove the old one six more years. Somewhere along the way her muzzle went gray, and so did the spot over my left ear that my hairdresser now calls a feature. We don't ride much anymore. Most evenings I sit on an upturned bucket by her stall while she works on her hay and the cat works on her back. Nobody says anything. It's still the best part of my day.
posts.first: I have a coffee can in the tack room full of her old mane braids from shows in the early years. I keep meaning to throw them out. Every spring when I clean the tack room I open the lid, look at them for a while, and put the can back on the shelf.

posts.caption: Spring is when it started. A new horse moved into the stall next to hers, and she has not forgiven any of us for that decision. She pins her ears at him over the divider every morning at feeding. She swishes her tail at the farrier on principle. She walked the whole trail ride Sunday with her nose half a step ahead of every other horse. Then we got back to the barn, I picked out her feet, and she rested her chin on my shoulder for a full minute. Don't tell anyone. She'd deny it.
posts.first: I had a mare in my twenties who only let one person catch her in the field, and it wasn't me. It was a retired mailman who boarded two stalls down. She walked right up to him every single time. I paid her board for nine years.
